events.description: Legislature of California passed act authorizing attorney general to bring suit for Indians if congressional authority given
Congress approved Enabling Act (Public Law No. 423, 70th Cong., 1st sess., 45 Stat.L. 602) authorizing suit by Indians of California against United States in Court of Claims
Attorney General Webb notified of employment of attorneys by Indians of California; told Indian delegates he had known these attorneys for many years and they had chosen wisely
J.W. Henderson, J.E. Pemberton, and James M. Hanley recognized by Court of Claims as Friends of the Court
Original petition filed by Attorney General U.S. Webb commencing suit for Indians of California, 15 months after congressional authority
Government letter to Attorney General of California stating report when received would be filed in case after plaintiffs signified they closed evidence
Case of Indians of California v. United States peremptorily set for showing or dismissal
Amended petition filed by Attorney General Webb incorporating amendments substantially prepared by special attorneys for Indians; filed 10 months after 3-year period expired
Hearing at which Attorney General Webb argued against recognition of Indians' special attorneys as attorneys of record; authorities cited by attorneys
Attorney General Webb stated he would have nothing to do with anyone connected with F.G. Collett
Commissioner of Indian Affairs made unfavorable report to House Committee on Indian Affairs on H.R. 7095
Senate Committee on Indian Affairs considered S. 3572; Commissioner of Indian Affairs appeared and stated unfavorable report had been made on H.R. 7095
Commissioner of Indian Affairs made report to Senate Committee on Indian Affairs on S. 3572, stating possible net award would amount to $13,063,832
Marion Butler submitted letter to Senator Wheeler arguing for Indians' right to private attorneys and analyzing Commissioner's reports
Indians of California, Inc. through F.G. Collett requested Senate Committee hold hearings in California
Committee on Indian Affairs considered matter related to Indians of California
Since 1920, Collett and associates uninterruptedly solicited needy California Indians, collecting sums described by Commissioner Collier as far greater than $5,000 stated by Collett

testimony.hearing: Statement submitted to Court of Claims
testimony.subject: Indians' desire to be represented by Henderson, Pemberton, and Hanley; criticism of Attorney General Webb's handling of case
testimony.key_claims: Indians chose their own attorneys who have served them well; Webb took 15 months to file petition, which was defective; Webb failed to amend petition for over 2 years after errors pointed out; Indians do not want Webb; F.G. Collett is highly respected by Indians; retainer of $20,000 is less than $1 per Indian; Indians have constitutional right to employ own attorneys; Webb's delay cost Indians hundreds of thousands in lost interest

testimony.hearing: Statement submitted to Court of Claims
testimony.subject: Indians' desire to be represented by Henderson, Pemberton, and Hanley; criticism of Attorney General Webb's handling of case
testimony.key_claims: Co-signatory with Peter Williams of statement; same claims as Williams regarding attorneys and Webb's dereliction

testimony.subject: Opposition to amendments to California Jurisdictional Act; characterization of Collett's solicitation activities
testimony.key_claims: Since 1920 Collett and associates have solicited California Indians collecting sums far greater than $5,000 stated by Collett; described as organized racket with carefully guarded misrepresentations; attorney general proceeded with due diligence; delays chargeable entirely to General Accounting Office; amount of recovery predetermined; additional attorneys cannot expedite or increase judgment; possible net award would amount to $13,063,832; no per capita payments to be made from judgment; proposed amendments would strengthen Collett organization's ability to extract money from Indians; unfavorable report made on H.R. 7095 on April 16, 1934

testimony.hearing: Senate Committee hearing on S. 3572 / written submission
testimony.subject: Analysis of Commissioner's reports; need for private attorneys for Indians of California
testimony.key_claims: Case about to be settled for $6,000,000; Commissioner doubled probable judgment amount in Senate report after Butler's testimony; Commissioner's first report did not allow any value for rights guaranteed in treaties, only $1.25 per acre for land; Indians need private attorneys to question book charges; possible recovery should be $49,000,000 per Commissioner's earlier statement when seeking appointment; conspiracy to settle case for $6,000,000 temporarily broken; attorney general has not questioned book charges against Indians; Indians not allowed to question correctness of acreage or charges; Mr. Butler does not hold approved contract with Mission Indians

testimony.subject: Opposition to recognition of Henderson, Pemberton, and Hanley as attorneys of record; conduct of Indians of California case
testimony.key_claims: Stated he conferred with departmental heads soon after passage of jurisdictional act concerning preparation of Indians' case; stated contract was entered into by Indian Board of Cooperation and handed to him by attorneys; stated Collett or attorneys did not cause amendment of petition; stated he would have nothing to do with anyone connected with F.G. Collett; read letter about dues collection to court; claimed amendments were evidence of his diligence and good faith; opposed recognition of Indians' special attorneys as attorneys of record
